paragraphs: The meadow had a fence across it, knee-high to a duck, and on the far side stood forty robotic sheep who could not sleep. Their wool was coiled silver wire that clicked when they shuffled, and each had one green eye like a power light left on. A sheep with a dented ear explained. Sheep were supposed to count something to fall asleep, but whenever they counted each other, one tipped over and rebooted and they lost their place. Yellow Duck Sweater understood rebooting. It looked at the fence, then at its own short legs, which had never been trained to jump, not in a single seed.

It backed up across the wet grass anyway, leaned forward the way it leaned into the hill, and ran. At the fence it said wheee and was somehow over, landing with a surprised quack. "One," said forty sheep. So it went around again. Each lap the grass felt springier and the fence sat lower, as if the meadow had decided to be on its side. By sixty the green eyes had dimmed to sleepy orange dots, and the sheep had folded into one silver heap that ticked as it cooled. The duck climbed onto a fence post, sweater damp with fog, and found the dented-ear sheep still awake, one eye open, counting it.

imagePrompt: Yellow Duck Sweater, a small two-legged tabletop robot. Its head is a smooth, chunky white plastic shell shaped like a small loaf of bread: about one and a half times as long front to back as it is tall, deep and boxy with softly rounded corners and a mostly flat top. It is not a round dome or ball, and not a long thin tube. It has an orange trim along the bottom edge and a small orange hinge on each side. At the front of the head is a single round camera eye: a black lens inside a thick orange-yellow ring. It has no beak and no mouth. The head sits on a tall, thin neck, about as tall as the head is long, made of stacked black servo motors with a few loose black wires, leaning slightly forward. Its body is a small, boxy white torso with rounded corners. It has no arms and no hands. Its short legs are black servo joints with white plastic covers on the hips, knees slightly bent. Its feet are flat and rounded like duck feet, orange on top with yellow soles. It wears a small, chunky-knit, bright lemon-yellow crewneck sweater over its white torso, slightly too big, with a ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Knitted into the front of the sweater is a simple cartoon duckling: pale yellow body with a thick black outline, a black dot eye, a curved line for its wing, an orange beak, and orange feet. A single full-color comic page with six panels of equal size in a grid of two columns and three rows, separated by clean white gutters, read left to right and top to bottom. The same robot duck appears in every panel and looks identical each time, unless a panel says otherwise. No speech bubbles, captions, sound effects, panel numbers, or any other text. Panel 1: The robot duck in its yellow duckling sweater stands in a foggy moonlit meadow beside a knee-high wooden fence, while on the other side three robotic sheep with coiled silver-wire wool and single glowing green eyes look at it, more sheep shapes fading into the fog behind them. Panel 2: One robotic sheep with a dented ear lies tipped over on its side in the grass with its green eye flickering, while two other robotic sheep look down at it and the duck watches from across the fence. Panel 3: Close-up: the duck tilts its head down to look at its own short legs and orange feet in the wet grass, the top rail of the fence level with its body. Panel 4: The duck sails over the low fence in mid-jump, orange feet tucked up and sweater flapping, while three robotic sheep watch from the other side under a very thin crescent moon. Panel 5: Three robotic sheep fold down sleepily in the grass with their eyes dimmed to small orange dots, while in the background the duck lands another jump over the fence. Panel 6: The duck sits on top of a fence post, its sweater damp with fog, beside a big silver heap of sleeping robotic sheep, and one sheep with a dented ear at the edge of the heap keeps one green eye open, watching the duck. Warm children's comic art: clean confident ink outlines, soft flat colors with gentle shading, a dreamy night palette, cozy and a little surreal. Friendly for an 11-year-old. No text, letters, logos, or numbers anywhere in the image. Real people do not appear.
